title: How can separate devices help sign one transaction?
dek: Your laptop can prepare a payment while the keys stay on separate devices. A PSBT is the document they pass around to get it signed.

blocks.text: Suppose the keys needed to spend some bitcoin live on different devices. Your laptop can prepare the payment, but it cannot finish the job alone. The other devices need to inspect the transaction, find the keys they control and return their signatures. They may even be offline.

That leaves a practical problem: what do you send them? A bare unsigned transaction leaves out information a signer needs. A Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, or PSBT, packages the transaction with that information and gives each participant somewhere to put its contribution. BIP 174 defines the common format.

figure.title: Separate signatures, one transaction
figure.caption: Both signers worked from the same updated PSBT. Their copies can be brought together without either signer handing over a private key.

blocks.text: Start with the Creator. It chooses the inputs and outputs and writes the unsigned transaction into a new PSBT. At this point the document says which coins to spend and where they should go, but the extra information about those coins has yet to be filled in.

An Updater supplies what it knows: the outputs being spent, any scripts needed to spend them, and derivation paths that help a signing device find the right keys. In this example an additional update supplies the signature hash type, which tells the signer what its signature should commit to.

Now the document can branch. Both signers receive the same updated copy. Each adds its own signatures and returns a PSBT. A Combiner brings the additions together. Nobody needs to wait for the other signer to finish before starting, and neither signer needs the other’s private keys.

blocks.title: Follow a PSBT through the handoffs
blocks.caption: Choose a stage to see what the document contains. The two signers work independently; the Combiner collects their contributions.

blocks.text: Creator, Updater, Signer and Combiner are jobs, rather than separate boxes you must buy. A wallet may perform several jobs. A signing device can also add information it knows. The format lets those jobs be divided between programs without requiring every program to know how the others work.

The example follows one route through those jobs. BIP 174 also describes arrangements such as manual CoinJoin and multisignature wallets. A PSBT can travel as a binary file or as Base64 text; the participants need to agree on the transaction and the format, rather than on a particular way of sending it.

A signing device can give its owner a chance to inspect the payment. How much is being spent? Where is it going? What is the fee? The PSBT carries information about the previous outputs so that a signer can work out those amounts. Derivation paths can also help it recognise change returning to its own wallet.

blocks.title: What the signer can show
blocks.caption: The amounts come from the document. Input 0 includes its full previous transaction; input 1 supplies only a witness UTXO record, so the displayed fee depends on that claimed amount.

blocks.text: Receiving information is not the same as establishing that it is true. For an input spending a pre-SegWit output, the Signer must hash the supplied previous transaction and check that its ID matches the one being spent. Otherwise a convincing-looking record could describe the wrong coins.

blocks.title: Does this previous transaction match?
blocks.caption: Hash the supplied transaction and compare it with the reference in the payment being signed.

blocks.text: SegWit has a less obvious trap. BIP 174 describes an attack in which a user is persuaded to sign repeatedly while the claimed amounts of other inputs change. A signature covering only its own input’s amount cannot settle the fee for the whole transaction. The BIP notes that many wallets request full previous transactions for SegWit inputs too.

A Signer must use the UTXOs supplied in the PSBT and only add data. It does not have to support every kind of input. Its contribution is a partial signature attached to an input, identified by the public key that made it. Other signatures can sit beside it without overwriting it.

Collecting signatures does not immediately produce the transaction that the network expects. First the Input Finalizer arranges the collected pieces into each input’s final scriptSig, witness, or both. Think of the PSBT as the work in progress and these final fields as the assembled result.

blocks.title: After assembly
blocks.caption: The input keeps its UTXO information and gains the final scripts. Partial signatures, paths and other completed working material are cleared.

blocks.text: That cleanup is deliberate. Once an input has its final scripts, the separate ingredients are no longer needed there. The Finalizer should clear everything except the UTXO records and fields it does not understand. If a sighash type was specified, it must refuse to finalize signatures that use a different one.

The Transaction Extractor then copies the final scripts into a network transaction. If an input is still incomplete, it must leave the PSBT untouched. This is the last handoff: the result can now leave the signing workflow as a transaction, rather than as a document asking for more work.

There is another useful check at the merge. The Combiner must reject PSBTs for different transactions. Combining information is only meaningful when everybody has been working on the same payment. For compatible contributions, the order of combination does not matter; conflicting records need separate treatment.

The format gives each piece of information a home. A global map holds transaction-wide information. Each input and each output gets its own map as well. Inside a map, records have keys and values: a key says what the information means, and its value holds the information itself.

blocks.title: The document before anyone adds to it
blocks.caption: The Creator has supplied the unsigned transaction. The input and output maps are still empty.

blocks.text: A record’s key can include extra identifying data. For a partial signature, that extra data is the signer’s public key. This is how an input can hold several signatures of the same record type: each has a different full key. Repeating an identical key in one map would make the document invalid.

blocks.title: Two signatures can share a record type
blocks.caption: The public key distinguishes one signer’s partial signature from the other’s.

blocks.summary: The byte format and validation rules

blocks.text: A PSBT begins with five bytes: the letters *psbt* followed by `0xff`. Then come key-value maps, one global map followed by one map per input and one per output of the transaction. Each map is a list of records, each with a key and a value, and ends with a single zero byte.

Each key is a type number, sometimes followed by key data. A map can hold several records of the same type as long as their full keys differ. That is how one input can carry several signatures at once: each partial signature’s key includes the public key that made it.

The global map holds the transaction being built, in its old serialization and with every scriptSig and witness empty. A version 0 PSBT without it is invalid. Within a map every key must be unique, and a PSBT with a duplicated key is invalid too. More generally, if any key or value does not match the format its type specifies, the whole PSBT must be considered invalid.

The decoder behind this page rejects all twenty invalid PSBTs that BIP 174 lists, from a missing output map to a duplicated key, and accepts the ten valid ones, keeping every record when it writes them back out. Each invalid case is a rule made concrete: a duplicated key, a filled scriptSig in the unsigned transaction, an unsigned transaction written with witness serialization, and, in twelve of the twenty, a key or value that does not match its type’s format.

A device will eventually encounter a field that was added after its software was written. BIP 174 requires signers to ignore unfamiliar types and pass them through. The device can do its own job without erasing information another participant needs. Finalization preserves those unknown fields too.

blocks.title: Keep what you do not understand
blocks.caption: The dashed records are unfamiliar to this decoder. Combining the documents preserves them because their full keys differ.

blocks.text: An unknown PSBT version is a different situation. The parser should stop immediately: it cannot assume that it understands the document’s rules. Version 2 PSBTs and Taproot fields are defined in other proposals. This chapter follows BIP 174’s version 0, with field names taken from the shared type registry.

That leaves a practical problem: what do you send them? A bare unsigned transaction leaves out information a signer needs. A Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, or PSBT, packages the transaction with that information and gives each participant somewhere to put its contribution. BIP 174 defines the common format.
BIP 174 was assigned in 2017 and is recorded as deployed in the pinned source. The example replays published PSBTs; it does not create signatures, hold keys or broadcast a transaction.
